hints: Recall the three products always formed when any Group 2 nitrate is heated strongly, and think about which one contains the metal.
walkthrough:
Remember the Group 2 nitrate pattern**
You have seen this family before. Every Group 2 nitrate breaks down in the same way on heating to give a white metal oxide solid, brown $\text{NO}_2$ gas and $\text{O}_2$ gas. So for strontium you already know the skeleton is $\text{Sr(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow \text{SrO} + \text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$.

Balance atoms carefully**
Count nitrogens. There are two nitrates on the left, so you need $2\text{NO}_2$ on the right. Then balance oxygens. Left has 6 O atoms, right has $1 + 4 = 5$ from $\text{SrO} + 2\text{NO}_2$, leaving one O atom to come from $\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$. That gives $\text{Sr(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow \text{SrO} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$.

hints: Think about what thermal stability means in practice, a more stable nitrate needs a higher temperature before it decomposes.
Compare the $\text{M}^{2+}$ ions down the group from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, what happens to ionic radius while charge stays 2+.
Link the polarising power of the cation to how much it distorts the electron cloud of the large $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion and weakens N-O bonds.
walkthrough:
State the trend clearly**
Picture heating $\text{Mg(NO}_3)_2$ and $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$ side by side. Magnesium nitrate decomposes very easily at relatively low temperature, barium nitrate needs much stronger heating. So stability increases going down the group with increasing atomic number.

Track the cation size**
All the ions are $2+$, so charge is constant. Going down from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ to $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ you are adding electron shells, so ionic radius increases and charge density falls. A small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is highly concentrating in charge, a large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is much more diffuse.

Connect polarisation to decomposition**
Think of the small, highly charged cation pulling hard on the electron cloud of the $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion next to it. That distortion, called polarisation, weakens the N-O bonds inside nitrate and helps it split into $\text{O}^{2-}$ plus $\text{NO}_2$. A larger cation down the group polarises less, distorts $\text{NO}_3^-$ less, so more heat is needed and stability is greater.

Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2 with increasing atomic number.
Down the group cationic radius increases / ion size increases.
Larger cation causes less polarisation / distortion of the $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion, so the nitrate is harder to break down.

hints: Use the statement that amides follow the same stability pattern as nitrates, then place Ca above Ba in Group 2.
walkthrough:
Transfer the nitrate logic to amides**
You are told the variation is similar to nitrates, so stability must still increase down the group. Calcium sits above barium, so $\text{Ca(NH}_2)_2$ is the less stable one, like $\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$ is less stable than $\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$. That means calcium amide decomposes more readily.

Justify with ion size**
The reason is identical. $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ with the same 2+ charge, so it has higher charge density and greater polarising power. It distorts the $\text{NH}_2^-$ ion more strongly, making decomposition easier.
Final answer: Calcium amide decomposes more readily than barium amide because $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has a smaller ionic radius / greater charge density than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$.

hints: Start by listing atoms in $\text{Ba(NH}_2)_2$, $\text{Ba}_3\text{N}_2$ and $\text{NH}_3$, then look for the smallest multiplier that balances Ba first.
walkthrough:
Balance the metal first**
Write the skeleton $\text{Ba(NH}_2)_2 \rightarrow \text{Ba}_3\text{N}_2 + \text{NH}_3$. Barium appears as 1 on the left and 3 on the right in $\text{Ba}_3\text{N}_2$, so put a 3 in front of $\text{Ba(NH}_2)_2$. Now Ba balances.

Finish N and H together**
With $3\text{Ba(NH}_2)_2$ you have 6 N and 12 H on the left. $\text{Ba}_3\text{N}_2$ uses 2 N, leaving 4 N and 12 H, which is exactly $4\text{NH}_3$. So $3\text{Ba(NH}_2)_2 \rightarrow \text{Ba}_3\text{N}_2 + 4\text{NH}_3$ balances fully.

hints: Count valence electrons on N in $\text{NH}_2^-$ to find the total number of electron pairs around nitrogen.
Split those pairs into bonding pairs to H and lone pairs, then recall the basic tetrahedral arrangement.
Remember the repulsion order lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair and how two lone pairs squeeze the H-N-H angle.
walkthrough:
Count electron pairs on nitrogen**
Nitrogen brings 5 valence electrons, each H shares 1 electron, and the 1- charge adds 1 more. That gives 8 electrons around N, or 4 pairs. Two pairs are used to bond to the two H atoms, leaving two lone pairs. So you have 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs.

Get the electron geometry**
Four pairs of electrons arrange themselves tetrahedrally to stay as far apart as possible. If all four were bonding, the angle would be the perfect tetrahedral $109.5^{\circ}$. Here the shape of atoms is bent or V-shaped because only two corners hold H atoms, similar to water.

Apply lone pair repulsion**
Lone pairs are held closer to N and spread out more, so they push harder than bonding pairs. The order is lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair. With two lone pairs squeezing together, the $\text{H-N-H}$ angle is compressed from $109.5^{\circ}$ down to about $104-105^{\circ}$, just like in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Final answer: Bond angle $104-105^{\circ}$.
N has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, giving a tetrahedral electron-pair arrangement.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the H-N-H angle from $109.5^{\circ}$.
